# Describing data II {.hero #s02-descriptives}

::: {.sem-mark data-sem="2"}
Seminar 2 · Descriptive statistics
:::

Averages are opinions about what "typical" means.

::: {.lede}
The worksheet asks for the mean, the median, the mode and the standard deviation of the same data. That is not busywork — each answers a different question, and they disagree exactly when the answer matters most.
:::

## A bound that holds for *any* shape {.sim-slide #cheb-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 2 · Chebyshev
:::

::: {.lede-min}
Chebyshev promises at least $1 - 1/k^2$ of any distribution lies within $k$ standard deviations. No normality, no symmetry, no assumptions at all.
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-text}
```{webr-r}
k <- 2        # <-- how many SDs
n <- 20000

# a wildly skewed population, nothing like normal
x  <- rexp(n, rate = 1)^2
mu <- mean(x); s <- sd(x)

actual <- mean(abs(x - mu) <= k * s)
bound  <- 1 - 1/k^2

round(c(actual = actual, chebyshev = bound), 3)
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
The bound holds, but loosely — that is the price of assuming nothing. Swap `rexp(n, 1)^2` for `rnorm(n)` and the gap widens further: for a normal, $k = 2$ captures 95%, not the 75% Chebyshev guarantees.
:::
